pages.title: Title
pages.summary: Market Efficiency — definitions, tests, anomalies, limits to arbitrage, and the 3Com/Palm case.

pages.title: What this deck covers
pages.summary: TOC: defining efficiency; three forms & tests; random walks & martingales; anomalies; multifactor models; finding factors; anomalies in detail; efficiency debate & limits to arbitrage; Lamont–Thaler case study.

pages.title: Market efficiency means…
pages.summary: P_t = E_t[Σ d_{t+k}/(1+r)^k]. All available info in expectations; right discount rate; quick, right-sized reaction to news; no free lunch. Hidden assumption: 'correct' presumes an asset pricing model.

pages.title: What information?
pages.summary: Nested sets: past prices ⊂ public ⊂ private ⟹ weak / semi-strong / strong forms. Venn diagram of nested ellipses.

pages.title: Grossman–Stiglitz paradox
pages.summary: If prices reflect everything, nobody is paid to gather information — then who makes them efficient? Resolution: prices reflect info up to where marginal benefit = marginal cost. Operational: deviations must exceed information + trading costs to count.

pages.title: The joint hypothesis problem
pages.summary: Can never be sure of inefficiency — risk may be mismeasured. Efficiency is not testable alone; tested jointly with a model of expected returns. Why expect efficiency at all: arbitrage forces.

pages.title: Weak form
pages.summary: Prices reflect past prices (Fama 1991: 'return predictability' broadly, incl. D/P, E/P, size, BE/ME). Technical analysis earns nothing. Questions: over/under-reaction? seasonals? within costs?

pages.title: Semi-strong form & event studies
pages.summary: Prices reflect all public info ⟹ fundamental analysis earns nothing. Event study: average CAR around announcements. Keown–Pinkerton takeover figure: run-up before announcement (leakage), jump at t=0 from ~12% to ~26%, flat after — rapid incorporation.

pages.title: Strong form
pages.summary: Prices reflect ALL info, incl. private — even insider trading earns nothing. Hierarchy: strong ⟹ semi-strong ⟹ weak.

pages.title: Martingales
pages.summary: E[P_{t+1}|history]=P_t — the fair game; best forecast of tomorrow's price is today's; increments serially uncorrelated. But no risk adjustment: neither necessary nor sufficient for efficiency; drift can be a risk premium.

pages.title: The random walk hypothesis (RW1)
pages.summary: P_t = μ + P_{t−1} + ε_t, ε iid(0,σ²). E[P_t|P0]=μt+P0; Var=σ²t — both linear in time. Independence ⟹ even nonlinear functions of increments unforecastable.

pages.title: Weaker RW hypotheses
pages.summary: RW2: independent, not identically distributed (heteroskedasticity ok). RW3: uncorrelated but dependent increments (e.g. volatility clustering: Cov(ε²_t,ε²_{t−k})≠0). Constant discount rates + efficiency ⟹ RW at short horizons ⟹ short-horizon tests mitigate the joint-hypothesis problem.

pages.title: The autocorrelation coefficient
pages.summary: r_it = γ0 + γ1k·r_{i,t−k} + ε. Under iid, autocorrelation = regression slope; ρ² = share of variance explained by the lag.

pages.title: A striking empirical pattern
pages.summary: Short-horizon autocorrelation: individual stocks NEGATIVE; portfolios POSITIVE. Resolution: large positive cross-autocorrelations — some stocks' past returns predict other stocks' futures.

pages.title: Decomposing the portfolio autocovariance
pages.summary: Cov(R_mt,R_m,t−k) for EW portfolio = (1/n²)Σ own-autocovariances + cross-autocovariances. Own terms small negative; portfolio positive ⟹ cross terms large positive (large stocks lead small).

pages.title: Does predictability mean inefficiency?
pages.summary: Not necessarily: microstructure (bid–ask bounce, nonsynchronous trading) can generate it spuriously. Predictable components tiny at short horizons but up to 40% of 2–10yr return variance; 3–5yr returns negatively autocorrelated (FF 1988a). Caveats: low power; bubbles vs mean-reverting expected returns — joint hypothesis again.

pages.title: The market anomalies
pages.summary: Anomaly = strategy with high returns without much risk (raises the frontier Sharpe above the market's). Recipe: sort on observable characteristics; measure average returns; mind transactions costs.

pages.title: If yes: three rival readings
pages.summary: 1 Risk (fair compensation — but measured how?). 2 Inefficiency — not yet: could be data mining or bad risk measurement. Even with no risk found: peso problem, or wrong measure.

pages.title: General ideas in asset pricing
pages.summary: Pays in bad times ⟹ attractive ⟹ low E[r]; pays in good times ⟹ high E[r]. CAPM: good/bad times = market return. But GNP, recessions, inflation matter too ⟹ multifactor models.

pages.title: Consumption-based models
pages.summary: Dynamic consumers price assets by marginal utility: price = E[discounted payoff, MU as discount]. Risk correction = covariance with consumption; assets that pay badly in recessions are riskier.

pages.title: APT and ICAPM
pages.summary: APT (Ross 1976): factor structure + no arbitrage ⟹ E[r] linear in loadings; silent on factor identity. ICAPM (Merton 1973): state variables that shift investment opportunities carry hedging premia; theory names the factors. Method 1 is APT-ish; methods 2–3 lean on ICAPM.

pages.title: Three ways to find factors
pages.summary: 1 statistical (factor analysis / PCA); 2 macro variables; 3 firm characteristics. For each: advantage, disadvantage, example, evidence.

pages.title: Method 1: statistical factors
pages.summary: Best factor estimates, APT-consistent; but unidentified factors, overfits noise. Roll–Ross 1980; Connor–Korajczyk 1988. 3–5 US factors; insensitive after five. Factor-analysis weights: min w'Σw s.t. unit loading on one factor, zero on others.

pages.title: Method 1: principal components
pages.summary: PC1 = max-variance unit-norm combination = top eigenvector; PC2 orthogonal runner-up; rescale weights to sum to 1. After ~5 PCs, results insensitive.

pages.title: Method 2: macro factors
pages.summary: Intuitive, ICAPM-consistent; but unanticipated changes hard to measure, no covariance-matrix link. CRR 1986 five: industrial production growth, ΔE[inflation], unexpected inflation, default premium, term premium. Consumption and oil add nothing.

pages.title: Implementation: two-step
pages.summary: Step 1 TS regression on factors → betas; Step 2 cross-section of average returns on betas → premia λ. CRR: 5-yr rolling loadings on size portfolios, 12 monthly cross-sections, Fama–MacBeth mean test.

pages.title: Reading the CRR numbers
pages.summary: MP premium annualized: 11.756·12/10 = 14.1%/yr vs ≈6.5% market premium. Market index premium insignificant once macro factors enter. Question: APT motivation for macro series that need not drive the covariance matrix?

pages.title: Method 3: firm characteristics
pages.summary: Intuitive, covariances needn't be constant, returns measure surprises, empirically strongest; but data mining / mispricing concerns. FF 1993/1996: Mkt−rf, SMB, HML; premia = average factor returns. Question: ICAPM motivation?

pages.title: The size effect
pages.summary: Hawawini–Keim 1995, VW size deciles 1951–89: smallest 19.8%/yr (β 1.17, $9.7m) → largest 11.9% (β 0.95, $3,983m). Betas too flat to explain the spread. Mispricing or missing risk.

pages.title: The January effect
pages.summary: Small-firm premium by month: Jan ≈0.70% dwarfs other months; ~3/4 of the premium in the first five days of January. Tax-loss selling (but international evidence), window dressing, new-year capital. Why no December front-running?

pages.title: Other seasonals
pages.summary: Monday negative, Wed–Fri positive; weekend effect (Friday close→Monday drop, volume higher Friday); turn-of-month and pre-holiday returns. Lakonishok–Smidt 1988 review + data-mining discussion.

pages.title: Contrarian strategies
pages.summary: DeBondt–Thaler 1985/87: rank on past 3 years; losers beat winners over the next 1–5 years (CAR figure: losers +≈0.30, winners −≈0.10 over 60 months).

pages.title: Contrarian: two explanations
pages.summary: Overreaction (behavioral) vs risk (losers riskier). Risk accounting: variance/CAPM regressions, payoff timing vs cycle, catastrophe risk. Past returns are noisy proxies for expected returns ⟹ move to D/P, E/P.

pages.title: Value and growth
pages.summary: Value (high B/M, C/P, E/P) dramatically outperforms growth. Rational: distress factor, fallen angels. Irrational: glamour stampede depresses growth's future returns; neglect raises value's.

pages.title: Momentum
pages.summary: 3–12 month relative winners keep beating losers — opposite of the 3–5yr contrarian result. Underreaction or risk? Next week's lecture.

pages.title: Shleifer's three arguments
pages.summary: For efficiency: rational investors; random irrationality cancels; arbitrageurs discipline correlated irrationality. Rebuttals: documented biases; correlated errors (framing, loss aversion, over/underreaction); arbitrage is limited in practice.

pages.title: Limits to arbitrage
pages.summary: No close substitutes (risky arbitrage); strategies can crater; short horizons force small positions; costs and liquidity vanish when needed; short-sale constraints. Shleifer–Vishny 1997: clients pull money after losses — arbitrageurs most constrained exactly when mispricing is widest.

pages.title: Data mining
pages.summary: Try 100 random series against returns: ≈5 'significant' t-stats by construction (histogram figure). Great backtests ≠ future profits; out-of-sample testing is the discriminator.

pages.title: So, how efficient is the market?
pages.summary: Three questions for any predictability: rational premium variation (conditioning info, omitted APT factor, consumption covariance)? irrational mispricing (psychology + price impact + failed arbitrage)? or chance (data mining)? Test out of sample.

pages.title: Lamont–Thaler: carve-outs
pages.summary: Law of one price: identical claims, identical prices; no model needed — no joint hypothesis. Equity carve-outs 1996–2000 present near-arbitrage violations; few cases, large mispricings.

pages.title: 3Com and Palm
pages.summary: 3/2/00 IPO: Palm closed $95.06; each 3Com share owned 1.5 Palm shares ⟹ implied ≥ $142.59; 3Com traded at $81.81. Stub = 81.81 − 142.59 = −$60.78/share ⟹ non-Palm 3Com valued at −$25 billion.

pages.title: The trading strategy
pages.summary: 3Com had announced the spin-off ⟹ buy 1 3Com, short 1.5 Palm, wait <1 year: buying a ≥0 asset for −$60.78. Not exactly riskless, but close; short horizon helps. L–T answers: (1) real mispricing — yes (options evidence); (2) enforcement blocked by short-sale constraints; (3) who buys Palm? 'We hypothesize that they are morons.'

pages.title: Dysfunctional yet 'efficient'?
pages.summary: Fama's operational definition tolerates mispricing within transactions costs. If shorting is impossible, a stock can be infinitely overpriced yet the market 'efficient'. Either reject EMH-with-low-costs, or accept EMH but concede a poorly functioning market.

pages.title: The sample: constructing stubs
pages.summary: 18 carve-outs with announced distributions, 1996–2000. Six unambiguous negative stubs (all NASDAQ tech, 12/98–8/00): Creative/UBID −$74.81; HNC/Retek −$49.01; Daisytek/PFSWeb −$13.72; Metamor/Xpedior −$5.26; 3Com/Palm −$62.68; Methode/Stratos −$20.86.

pages.title: The 3Com/Palm stub through time
pages.summary: Daily stub 3/2–9/18/00: −$63 at IPO, partial recovery after the 3/20 accelerated-distribution announcement, choppy April, climb after the 5/8 IRS approval, crosses zero early July, jumps positive at the 7/27 distribution, settles ≈+$10-15.

pages.title: Risk and return on stub trades
pages.summary: Parents beat issuers by 33% over ≈6 months from first negative stub to distribution announcement. Risk–return four times better than the market; grotesquely mispriced by the CAPM. Non-completion risks (IRS, takeover) don't touch the options-market evidence.

pages.title: Short-sale constraints
pages.summary: Not easily exploitable: borrowing shares can be hard or impossible; rebates negotiated, can go negative (short-seller pays daily). Stubs: negative rebates and unborrowable stock — the lending market didn't equilibrate.

pages.title: Options evidence: put–call parity
pages.summary: C−P = S−PV(X) (European); C−P > S−X (American, no dividends) ⟹ ATM calls above puts. Massively violated for Palm; synthetic shares ≠ actual shares — another law-of-one-price violation. Implied cost of borrowing Palm: 14% over two months ≈ 119%/yr.

pages.title: Lamont–Thaler conclusions
pages.summary: Ross's parrot ('arbitrage'). New issues unambiguously overpriced; prices wrong but not exploitably wrong; frictions — especially shorting costs — are key; unknown whether the phenomenon is widespread.

pages.title: Market efficiency: summary
pages.summary: Efficiency = prices reflect info GIVEN a model (joint hypothesis); operational test: deviations within costs. Evidence: small short-horizon autocorrelations (negative stocks / positive portfolios via cross-autocorrelations); long-horizon mean reversion, low power. Anomalies: size, seasonals, contrarian, value, momentum. Readings: rational factors, limited-arbitrage mispricing, or data mining. Lamont–Thaler: prices can be wrong without being exploitable.
